1:
Why the whole people bore one man's guilt opens the chapter, and Calvin will not let his answer stand. It seems very unaccountable, he says, that a whole people should be condemned for a private crime of which they had no knowledge; his first reply is that it is not new for the sin of one member to be visited on the body, and that if the reason escapes us it should be enough that transgression is imputed to Israel while the guilt lies on one. Then he objects against himself: all were ignorant of the theft, so the maxim that he who allows a crime is its perpetrator does not apply. He admits in the end that it is not clear why a private crime is imputed to the whole people, unless they had been slack before in punishing misdeeds, so that this man sinned the more boldly: weeds creep in stealthily and produce noxious fruits if not speedily torn up. Gill and Wesley state the fact without the difficulty: Gill that the deed was done by one and, not being discovered, was imputed to the whole; Wesley that the children of Israel means one of them by a usual figure, as what belonged to Judas is ascribed to the disciples.

On the names they correct one another from the versions. Keil notes that where this book has Achan the Chronicler has Achar, the liquids interchanged to allow a play upon the verb used later, so that Josephus spells it Acharos and one Greek codex Achar while another keeps Achan; and that Zabdi appears elsewhere as Zimri. Wesley records the same, and that Zerah was Judah's immediate son. Ellicott says only that Judah is distinguished in sacred history for great crimes as well as great achievements. Henry marks the conjunction that begins the story, the chapter opening with a but after all the promise of the last, and reads the sin as the one prohibition broken: at Jericho they were to spare no lives and take no treasure, and we read of no breach of the first, since there were none to whom they showed mercy, but compassion yielded while covetousness was indulged.

Where Ai stood they place variously. Gill calls it the next city of importance though smaller than Jericho, three miles off according to the Jews and four according to Abarbanel, and reports from Jerome that in his time only the site was shown. Clarke identifies it with the Hai of Genesis, ten or twelve miles north of Jericho, set on a hill and belonging to the Amorites. Ellicott asks instead why Ai should have been selected next at all, declines to answer, and observes only that the step after its capture was to set up the Ten Commandments on Mount Ebal.

Whether the scouts advised well they divide. Calvin allows that to reconnoitre the approaches was prudence, lest they hurry on at random and fall into an ambuscade, but doubts the rest, since to send a small band to take the city when the whole force must shortly advance seems ill judged. Ellicott finds in the phrase about not making all the people labour a side-glance at Israel's comment on the seven days' march round Jericho, which they thought useless labour, being unable to appreciate its lesson. Wesley reads the miscarriage as providence, so that their sin might be punished and they reformed with as little mischief as might be. On the rout Clarke says they presumed the men of Ai would open their gates; Ellicott calls it a natural reaction from overweening confidence to dismay, and explains Shebarim as the ravines below Ai; Gill says the loss was small but the shame great; and Wesley says they had not courage to strike a stroke, plain evidence that God had forsaken them, and a useful instruction to show them what they were when God left them.
6:
Why so small a loss prostrated the general they answer past numbers. Calvin puts the objection first: it ill became a courageous leader to be so cast down by the loss of thirty men, when by increasing his force a hundredfold it would not have been difficult to drive back an enemy weary with exertion. Yet the sorrow was not without cause, since the thought that the events of war are doubtful, which sustains the defeated, could not be entertained by Joshua, God having promised that they would always be victorious; so when success did not answer his hopes the only conclusion was that they had fought deprived of the promised assistance of God. Clarke reaches the same place by another road: it was not the slight discomfiture in itself but that the people melted and became as water, with little hope that they would make a stand. Henry says as much in a sentence: had it been but the common chance of war it would not have become a general to droop, but when God was angry it was his duty and honour to feel thus.

What the mourning rites signified they treat as more than custom. Gill says the rending was usual on hearing bad news, and Wesley that it testified sorrow for the loss felt, the mischief feared and the sin suspected, the whole day being spent in fasting and prayer. Calvin allows that the heathen used the same mode of expressing grief, but says it was specially appropriate in the pious when suppliantly deprecating God's wrath, since the rending and the dust contained a profession of repentance. Henry adds the posture, that Joshua fell to the earth on his face, not thinking it any disparagement to lie so low before the great God, and kept his eye toward the ark; and he makes him an example to princes in laying public calamity to heart, and a type of Christ, to whom his subjects' blood is precious.

Whether the complaint was blameworthy is the sharpest division here. Wesley says the words, though well intended, savour of human infirmity and fall short of the reverence and submission Joshua owed to God, and are recorded as instances that holy men were subject to like passions with ourselves. Clarke defends him: the expostulations have been too hastily blamed by some as savouring of too great freedom and impatience, whereas they are founded on God's own words in Deuteronomy and on the practice of Moses himself. Calvin divides the prayer instead of judging it whole: it is of a mixed nature, dictated partly by faith and the pure spirit of piety and partly by excessive perturbation, since in turning straightway to God and owning that the cure was prepared in the hand that inflicted the wound they are influenced by faith.

What Joshua feared and what he pleaded they separate. Calvin says he mentions another ground of fear, that the neighbouring nations, quiet till now because subdued or terrified, would resume confidence and attack; Ellicott says the thing was extremely probable in itself, apart from the supernatural character of the invasion. On the plea Gill says Joshua asks what he shall say for the comfort of Israel and in vindication of God's power and faithfulness, against the charge of weakness and unfaithfulness to his promises; Wesley, that the great name would be charged with inconstancy and inability, and that whatever happens we ought to pray that it be not blasphemed, the name of God being above every name. Ellicott turns from the plea to the man: these words and this behaviour are consistent with all we read of Joshua and confirm the notion that he was not naturally daring and adventurous but inclined to distrust his own powers, yet utterly indomitable in the discharge of his duty, a man of moral rather than physical courage. Keil records the prayer without comment.
10:
Whether God rebuked Joshua at all they answer in four degrees of severity. Clarke denies any rebuke: nothing in the prayer offended God, and there is no reprehension, only that this is no time for complaint when something else is indispensably necessary. Gill says God spoke not as refusing the supplication but as encouraging, strengthening and chiefly instructing him. Henry allows the humbling but limits it: Joshua did well to mourn under the tokens of God's displeasure, yet God called it enough, delighting not in grief beyond what qualifies penitents for pardon. Calvin makes the finest distinction: God reprimands him not for lying prostrate, the true method of obtaining pardon, but for excessive sorrow, and refers the censure to the future rather than the past, as if to say he had lain long enough and all sloth must now be abandoned. Wesley puts it in a line: this business is not to be done by inactive supplication but by vigorous endeavours; Ellicott notes only that the pronoun is emphatic.

Why the whole nation is charged when one man stole Calvin now handles differently than at the chapter's opening. He refers back to that discussion and withdraws: though they were not held guilty in their own judgment or that of others, the judgment of God which involved them in the same condemnation had hidden reasons, into which it may be lawful to inquire soberly but not to search with prying curiosity. He adds a rare example of clemency: the condemnation verbally extends to all, but punishment falls only on the single family polluted by the crime. Gill keeps the possibility of shared fault: though one only sinned, others might have known and connived; Wesley reads Israel as some or one of them; Clarke hears in the stealing a calculation: if his brethren did not see, God would either not see or not notice.

Why the spoil of this city was forbidden Ellicott explains from the law. The words of the covenant pledge that Jehovah is the God of Israel and made Israel the executioner of his wrath against idolaters; they must not treat as their own spoil the things defiled by idolatry, the applicable words being the Deuteronomic prohibition against desiring the silver or gold upon the graven images. The whole spoil of Canaan was not so treated, but concerning Jericho there were express orders, possibly because the city was especially defiled, so that no Israelite might appropriate any of it without becoming devoted himself. Clarke draws the same consequence from the word: whoever took of the thing doomed to destruction fell under the same condemnation; Wesley says they had put themselves out of God's protection and become liable to the destruction belonging to the accursed people; Keil says Israel could not stand until the accursed thing was destroyed.

What sanctifying the people required Calvin takes more strictly. Although the word has a wider meaning, he says, since the subject is the expiation of the people he has no doubt a formal rite is prescribed, and those who interpret it generally miss its full force; they were now brought into the divine presence, and needed purification lest they come unclean. The ceremony might be of little consequence in itself, but it had a powerful tendency to arouse a rude people: the external offering turned their thoughts to spiritual cleanness, and abstinence from lawful things reminded them of the purity required. They are forewarned, he adds, that each may examine himself, and the Lord proceeds step by step as if to give intervals for repentance, no other reason being imaginable for descending from tribe to family before reaching the man. Clarke reduces the command to washing and a proper disposition to hear the judgment, Wesley to purifying from the defilement all had in some sort contracted; Gill notes that the word up signifies not only rising from the ground but bestirring himself.
14:
How the criminal was discovered divides them, and both sides appeal to the same precedent. Clarke reports the Jewish conceits, the most rational being that the tribes, brought in their representatives before the high priest, were detected when the stone on the breastplate suddenly lost its lustre, which they call consulting God by Urim and Thummim; but he judges it most probable that the whole was determined by the lot, citing the election of Saul, where Benjamin was taken, then Matri, then Saul, the procedure being in the main entirely similar. Wesley agrees: the guilty are declared by the lot, disposed by the Lord according to Proverbs and cast in his presence before the ark. Ellicott denies it: nothing in the language, closely considered, suggests casting lots, and the parallel of Saul shows rather that the oracle of God was consulted, since they inquired and the Lord answered.

He then reconstructs the scene. We seem to see the high priest asking counsel after the judgment of Urim, as foretold in Numbers, with the elders standing at the door of the tabernacle, while the representatives of the tribes enter the sacred enclosure in succession and pass before him in awful silence, broken only by the voice of Jehovah pronouncing at intervals the names of Judah, Zarhite, Zabdi, Carmi, Achan. It must have been a terrible ordeal, he says, but all present must have felt that no human partiality or private animosity was seeking its victim: the Judge of all the earth was doing judgment. If the voice came from between the cherubim yet was heard to the outer court, then the arrest of Jordan, the overthrow of Jericho and the discovery of Achan are manifestations of one power.

That the record of the search is disturbed two of them grant and one denies. Keil observes that at verse seventeen we should expect the tribe or the families of Judah rather than the family; the plural stands in the Septuagint, the Vulgate and seven manuscripts, but he calls it a conjecture rather than the original reading, since the word is used generally or collectively. Clarke goes further with Kennicott, who sets the command against its execution: the command has four stages, tribes, families, households, man by man, but the narrative gives the third article as man by man and so doubles it, by households having certainly dropped out; six Hebrew copies and the Syriac preserve the true word. Wesley harmonises without emendation, taking family as the singular for the plural and man by man as the heads of the houses, not every individual, which the next verse proves.

Why the lot fell on Judah Henry presses as the point. That tribe was, and was to be, the most honourable and illustrious, so the discovery was an alloy to their dignity and a check to their pride: many there were who were its glories, but here was one that was its reproach. Judah was to have the first and largest lot in Canaan, which makes the offender less excusable, since he would not wait for his own share but broke in upon God's property; and Henry passes on the tradition that when the tribe was taken its valiant men drew their swords and would not sheathe them till the criminal was punished and they were cleared. Stranger still, he thinks, that Achan, conscious of guilt and watching the lot come nearer, had neither the wit to escape nor the grace to confess, his heart being hardened through the deceitfulness of sin until the lot said, Thou art the man. Of the sentence Gill notes that burning was one of the four capital punishments with the Jews and was ordered here because Jericho had been burnt, and Wesley that the folly wrought in Israel was sacrilege, scripture naming sin folly in opposition to the idle opinion of sinners, who esteem it their wisdom.
19:
What giving glory to God required they take four ways. Clarke reads it as a formula: make a thorough confession as in the presence of God, disguising no part of the truth, and in these very words the Jews adjured the man born blind, pretending that Christ was such a sinner that God would not work a miracle by him. Calvin makes the same identification and adds a reason peculiar to this case: the matter was already determined by lot, so that equivocation might have impaired the credit of the decision, and Joshua simply orders him to subscribe to the divine sentence. Wesley unfolds glory into four dishonoured attributes now to be owned: omniscience in knowing the sin, justice in punishing it, omnipotency obstructed, and the kindness to Israel that the wickedness eclipsed. Ellicott alone turns the verse forward: to tell Joshua is, in New Testament language, to tell Jesus, the only way confession can bring glory, since Joshua could pronounce nothing but death; and the Hebrew for confession also means thanksgiving, so acknowledgment of sin and mercy are not far apart.

Calvin turns the address into a lesson for the bench, and guards it. Joshua calls him son neither ironically nor hypocritically, but truly felt as a father toward one he had already doomed to death; judges are thereby taught so to temper severity that they do not lay aside humanity, and to be merciful without being reckless and remiss, in short to be as parents to those they condemn without substituting mildness for the sternness of justice. The counterfeit is near: many by fawning kindness throw criminals off their guard, pretending they mean to pardon, and then, the confession once extracted, hand them to the executioner. Joshua, having cited the criminal before God's tribunal, does not flatter him with a vain hope of pardon. Gill notes the humane manner shown to so great a criminal, a subject of his own and of the same religion; Wesley, that the inquisition sprang from no hatred of his person.

Whether the confession was repentance they divide. Clarke calls it a very honest and hearty confession and hopes the poor culprit escaped perdition; Wesley finds it sincere and ingenuous, loading the sin with just aggravations. Calvin refuses the inference: the simplicity was no sure indication of repentance, for overcome with terror he divulged what he would willingly have concealed, and it is no new thing for the wicked to become witnesses against themselves, not of their own accord but because God drags them against their will. Yet he grants what the words carry: thus and thus did I is emphatic, each part explained distinctly and in order, and Achan would not have said I have sinned had he not been conscious of sacrilege, so he pretended no mistake or want of thought.

The garment they cannot identify; the money they can. Gill reports Babylonish wool from Jarchi, or a garment of Shinar from Kimchi and Abarbanel, with Josephus calling it royal and interwoven with gold. Clarke cannot settle whether such robes were woven, embroidered or painted, citing Silius Italicus for the loom, Martial for the needle and Apuleius for paint, deciding for needlework after the loom; he prices the silver at about thirty pounds and the gold at about a hundred and thirteen. Ellicott supplies the one verbal argument: coveted is the word of the tenth commandment and of the Deuteronomic ban on desiring the spoils of idolatry, making it somewhat probable the whole came from an idol's shrine. Keil adds the trade note, that such cloaks were artistically worked in Babylon and spread far by commerce, Pliny recording that the city gave the practice its name. Clarke numbers the advance of the sin, by eye, heart, hand and dissimulation, where Wesley narrates it; and Calvin says the messengers ran not merely to obey Joshua but much more to appease the Lord.
24:
Whether Achan's children died with him is the hardest question here, and Clarke alone answers no. He rests it on the pronouns: the Hebrew says they stoned him and burnt them after they had stoned them, the singular in the first clause and the plural in the last leaving it doubtful. The versions divide. The Vulgate says all Israel stoned him and all he had was consumed with fire; the Septuagint, Syriac and Anglo-Saxon speak only of him and his goods; the Targum agrees with the Hebrew; the Arabic alone names the children; and two of De Rossi's manuscripts read him for them. He adds that all that he hath may refer to his goods, that the law forbids putting children to death for the fathers without proof of complicity, and that they were brought out only to see and fear.

Ellicott and Wesley take the opposite view, on opposite grounds. Ellicott holds all were destroyed together: for any other sin Achan must have suffered alone, but warning had been given that whoever took the devoted thing became devoted himself and made the camp devoted, so his whole establishment perished as part of Jericho. It is not necessary, he says, to assert complicity, since the cattle were no accomplices and perished; and the line is not continued in the Chronicles. Wesley grants the deaths and defends them three ways: their death was a debt owed to their own sins, which God may require when he pleases; a very few deaths at the beginning of a new empire prevented thousands who took warning; and they probably knew of the theft, Achan being the fifth from Judah and likely old enough for grown children.

Calvin neither softens the case nor explains it. It seems harsh, nay barbarous and inhuman, that young children without fault should be hurried to cruel execution; that dumb animals suffer so is less strange, since they were created for men and follow their owners' fate. He states the difficulty at full strength, that God here publicly punishes children for their parents, contrary to what he declares by Ezekiel, and answers only from the disproportion of knowledge: it penetrates more deeply than human intellect can, so we acquiesce in his decree rather than hurry to a precipice by presumption. It was not reckless hatred that slew them: circumcision, the infallible symbol of adoption, was engraved on their flesh, and yet he adjudges them to death; what remains but to acknowledge our weakness and submit to his incomprehensible counsel? Death may have proved a medicine, and if they were reprobate the condemnation could not be premature.

The execution was outside the camp for two reasons, Calvin says: that it not be tainted, since God always required some trace of humanity even in legitimate punishments, and that no defilement remain in it. The general stoning was a sign of detestation, all declaring they had no share in the crime; the heap served partly as a memorial and partly to keep anyone from gathering particles of gold or silver there, for though the gold of Jericho was claimed for God he would not have his sanctuary polluted by the proceeds of theft. Gill takes the heap for a monument of the place of execution and burial, such monuments being usual with heathens as with Jews, and cautions that God's turning from his anger means the effects ceased, there being properly no change in him; Keil notes only that sentence was pronounced again in the place of judgment. From the oxen, asses and sheep Calvin and Wesley alike infer that Achan had no colour of necessity, but an insatiable cupidity coveting stolen goods not for use but for luxury. Ellicott finds in the name a double play, the valley of trouble given for a door of hope, a pass from Jericho toward Jerusalem, from the city of destruction to the city of God.
